Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed randomized trial•April 20, 2026

Primary-care dementia screening did not improve family quality of life in COADS

Screening neither improved family quality of life nor increased measured psychological harm over two years.

Key quantitative results: At 24 months, combined screening versus control differences in SF-36 scores were −0.21 (95% CI −1.26 to 0.85) for physical health and 0.58 (−0.18 to 1.33) for mental health.

Clinical TrialsManagementCognitive assessment

Added September 7, 2026 · DOI:10.1001/jamainternmed.2026.0844; NCT03300180

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

These results concern cognitive screening pathways for older adults, not evaluation of symptomatic patients or blood-biomarker accuracy.

Study design

1,808 patient–family dyads in 29 primary-care clinics; adults ≥65; screening, screening plus diagnostic referral, or no-screening control.

Key quantitative results

  • At 24 months, combined screening versus control differences in SF-36 scores were −0.21 (95% CI −1.26 to 0.85) for physical health and 0.58 (−0.18 to 1.33) for mental health.
  • Only 62 screened patients (5.1%) screened positive; 10 (35.7%) in the screen-plus positive subgroup declined diagnostic follow-up.

What changed

A randomized study tests family benefit rather than assuming it follows detection.

Strength of evidence

Randomized pathway evidence with low detection yield.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Follow-up engagement matters to screening programs.

Field medical relevance

Separate detecting impairment from improving family outcomes.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Referral availability alone did not ensure uptake.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does a negative result mean symptomatic assessment is unnecessary?
No. The study addresses screening, not that clinical question.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Low positive-screen rate and incomplete diagnostic follow-up.
  • AD and related dementias; not exclusively biomarker-confirmed AD.

Primary source · DOI

Fowler NR, Perkins AJ, Gao S, et al. Benefits and harms of dementia screening for family members of older adults. JAMA Intern Med. Published April 20, 2026;186:689–700. doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2026.0844.
